decisions.reason: SOL preserves all facts while giving the ship’s movement a cleaner sentence.
Dropping the article before the title does not change the role or rank.
SOL preserves the comparison; “already” is not needed to convey that he achieved more.
SOL keeps the rarity claim in concise, natural English.
“Fuck” matches the source’s profanity, and the revised word order preserves the thought.
SOL drops the image of the rough current breaking around the ship.
“Prided himself” naturally conveys his self-assurance without changing the claim.
The Korean thought is singular; “I’m fucked” preserves its subject.
The omitted “In the end” adds no meaning to the arrival of the inevitable.
The ellipsis preserves the subordinate’s hesitation.
SOL preserves the slow turn and recognition without changing the action.
The shorter question keeps the same threat and voice.
The sentence break preserves Sudal’s deliberate repetition and pause.
“Recover the composure” keeps the sense while avoiding the clumsy “teaching him to rediscover.”
SOL preserves the elapsed time and the rhetorical question in natural dialogue.
The singular “He” fits the reported demand and preserves its meaning.
Deleting this drops the source’s “sure enough, it’s him” beat before the following explanation.
The following sentence identifies the shared referent, so the shorter phrasing preserves the point.
The fragment remains clear and preserves the characterization.
“Much the same sort” preserves the comparison and reads naturally.
The recast avoids a dangling description while retaining the young man’s appearance and habit.
“Those days” makes the past reference natural without changing the wistful recollection.
The preceding line identifies the skewers; the footnote preserves the Korean insult wordplay without repeating the food name.
SOL weakens “far, far above him” to a generic bigger figure, losing the source’s emphasis on status.
The Korean is conditional: if it is Cheongpung, he is a big shot among big shots.
“Popular opinion” and “ranked among the top three of all time” preserve the source’s public assessment.
“Spicy marinade” accurately preserves the requested seasoning.
The subordinate’s turning pale remains clear without the redundant speech tag.
“Emergency supply of drinking snacks” preserves the stash’s purpose in natural English.
“My cabin” preserves ownership without the awkward “cabin I use.”
The recast preserves the proposed escort and the joke about Taishan’s appetite.
The subordinate’s praise remains intact without the redundant “all right.”
“Gave him a thumbs-up” is the natural phrasing for the same gesture.
“Vanished” preserves the sudden disappearance of the smile.
Removing “all of a sudden” avoids repetition while preserving the sudden swell of misery.
“회의감” conveys futility or disillusionment, not the doubt SOL substitutes.
“Might” preserves the uncertainty in the conditional hope of arriving within a day.
The reordered phrasing preserves Sudal’s return to awareness and the old man’s appearance.
The interrupted address remains clear and natural in the exchange.
The old man’s echoing question remains intact.
The single ellipsis follows the project’s punctuation convention and preserves the pause.
Omitting “here” does not change where the Dragon King would come up for air.
“Now” is redundant with the sentence’s present context.
The Korean compares the forehead with other people’s; “twice its normal size” changes the reference point.
The article change does not alter the old master’s identity or the hoped-for encounter.
“Silence fell at once” preserves the immediate hush without the redundant sentence reference.
“Before him” adds no information to the stare.
The Korean calls him one of Murim’s human scum; SOL turns that into a general condemnation “for the good of Murim.”
The following dialogue makes clear that he replied; the tag is unnecessary.
The emphasized “the Namho” preserves his boastful claim to identity.
Removing the repeated name does not obscure who is remembering his youth.
The recast removes an awkward causal construction while preserving Sudal’s unfamiliarity with the name.
The Korean explicitly names Sudal as the one shocked; SOL replaces that subject with an implicit “him.”
“Then another two thousand” preserves the subordinate’s escalating, admiring tally.
The omitted “Sure” does not change the boast or its contrast between force and victory.
The source says whenever he sent a pigeon the sects moved; SOL changes this to “all I had to do,” adding a claim about ease.
The single ellipsis preserves the puzzled silence and follows the punctuation convention.
The source presents Namho as unapologetically confident; “pleased with himself” changes that attitude.
The single ellipsis preserves the reaction and follows the punctuation convention.
The conversational recast preserves the danger, hardship, and consequences of martial life.
The single ellipsis preserves the reaction and follows the punctuation convention.
“용한 의원” means a notably skilled physician; “famous” is more specific than the source supports.
The source says Sudal has already lost it, then specifies rage; SOL changes this to physical bodily failure.
The recast preserves his last thread of reason and the final question without awkwardly making his lips do the asking.
“Even” preserves the emphasis of asking why his forehead is swollen despite not learning the technique.
The single ellipsis preserves the reaction and follows the punctuation convention.
The unpossessed compound “Black Gold Bee hive” is natural and preserves which bee caused the sting.
The sentence split preserves the simultaneous action and Sudal’s dizziness.
The recast preserves the abandoned merchant ships and the forced route without changing the sequence.
“Going by the name Blood Monk” changes the source’s sobriquet into an alias; BASE correctly says he was known as Blood Monk.
The Korean describes people as uneducated; “uncultured” shifts the category to manners or refinement.
The idiomatic recast preserves Sudal’s frustration that things are still going wrong at the end.
The recast clarifies Sudal as the one fooled and insulted while preserving the old man’s powerlessness.
“To his subordinates” preserves the source’s explicit audience for Hyuk Mujin’s preaching.
The source identifies Ju Hwaran by the title Ten Dragons and Phoenixes; “one of” changes that designation to membership in a group.
“Watch everyone” preserves her monitoring behavior without the unnecessary “keep an eye on.”
The source says she mutters as if she wants people to hear; SOL asserts she speaks loudly, changing the cue and intent.
The source’s reason is the Pavilion Master’s comfort; SOL narrows that to rest.
The recast preserves the accumulated frustration and the five-day duration.
The source first says he drew the saber, then corrects that he only tried; SOL changes the first action to reaching.
Deleting the correction removes the source’s comic self-interruption: he drew it—or rather, tried to.
The fragment continues the corrected action and preserves the interruption’s timing; SOL merges the beats.
“After that rest” weakens the source’s emphasis that a thorough rest made him feel much better.
The split preserves the slow turn, Taekyung’s return, and Sudal looking up to answer.
The additional concise footnote explains the Korean insult wordplay and supports the retained *horo* rendering.
